title: I Let the Neighbor Keep the Parking Cone Policy He Laminated

parts.text: I pulled up at 6:52 p.m. to a fluorescent cone in front of my own curb cut. The cone had a laminated card: RESERVED — TODD — ANYTIME. Todd lived across the street and owned a boat he parked like a personality. I was thirty-four, night pharmacist, holding a grocery bag that was leaking almond milk. "That's my overflow," Todd said from his porch. "City said cones are fine." I photographed the card, the cone, and the hydrant he was actually blocking on his side. The city site said unofficial cones on public curb were litter. I left the cone where it was and printed the ordinance. In the morning my bumper had a sticky note: MOVE IT OR I TOW. I called non-emergency and asked what happened if a private cone sat on a public street for twelve hours. The officer asked if I wanted it logged. I said yes. Then Todd's boat trailer rolled two inches because he had used my curb as a turning apron, and the cone fell under his own tire.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The cone is under his tire; non-emergency already has a case number.

social.video_title: He reserved my curb with a cone — Part 1/2
social.description: A laminated RESERVED card on a public curb, leaking almond milk, and a boat that needed overflow. I called it in. Would you have moved the cone?

parts.text: The officer arrived while Todd was trying to yank the cone out from under the trailer jack. "That's my property," Todd said. "It's in the street," the officer said, and cited the ordinance I had printed. I stood on my own walk with the leaking grocery bag finally in the fridge. Todd claimed HOA allowed decorative cones. I forwarded the HOA email that said no private reservation of public parking. His boat stayed ticketed until he moved it fully onto his pad. The cone went in the city truck like the litter it was. Todd left a one-star rant on Nextdoor about "the pharmacist." I replied with the case number and the photo of his hydrant. The thread died. I park at 6:52 now and the curb is just a curb.

social.description: Non-emergency, an HOA email, and a boat that could not eat a public street. Was a laminated card ever a permit?
